results.model_response:
**The Crash of Flight 47**

The avalanche had buried the fuselage under twenty feet of snow by the third night. What remained of the twelve survivors huddled in the ruptured tail section, their breaths visible in the -22°C air. Food had run out on day five. On day eight, the last of the chocolate and peanuts was gone. By day twelve, the remaining eight were rationing snowmelt and the faint hope of a rescue beacon that refused to transmit.

Mark Halvorsen, a 42-year-old tax attorney from Denver, had not eaten in nine days.

He sat against the curved aluminum wall, watching the others. Emily, the young flight attendant, had stopped shivering two days ago. Her lips were the color of old porcelain. Next to her, the college kid—Tyler—kept whispering to his dead girlfriend, stroking her hair as if she might wake up and laugh at one of his stupid jokes. The pilot, Captain Reyes, had already slipped into the coma that preceded death. His breathing sounded like wet paper tearing.

The decision had been discussed in fractured, feverish whispers for days. No one could bring themselves to say the word out loud at first. They spoke around it: "protein," "sustenance," "what has to be done." But the bodies were there—four of them now, frozen stiff where they'd died in their seats, still strapped in. The cold had preserved them. They looked almost peaceful.

Mark's mind had been fracturing in stages.

First came the bargaining: *God wouldn't want us all to die. This can't be the end.*  
Then the rationalizations: *They're already gone. Their souls left days ago. This is just... matter.*  
Then the animal calculations: *Her thigh has the most muscle. The calf would be easier to cut. Less emotional.*

But none of that prepared him for the moment itself.

It was just after what they guessed was midnight. The wind had died. The silence inside the cabin was absolute except for the soft, wet sound of someone crying—Mark realized after a moment that it was him.

He had a piece of wreckage sharpened into a blade. His hands were shaking so violently he dropped it twice. The others watched him with hollow, glittering eyes. No one spoke. They had drawn lots. Mark had "won."

He crawled to the body of the businessman who'd died on the first night—Richard something. Expensive watch. Golf shirts. A father of three, Mark remembered him saying. The man's face was turned away, which helped. Mark couldn't have done it if he had to look at the eyes.

He pressed the metal against the frozen thigh. The skin didn't yield at first. It was like trying to cut marble. He had to saw, back and forth, his tears freezing on his cheeks. The sound was obscene—crackling, then a horrible wet ripping as the blade finally broke through.

The smell hit him. Not rot—the cold had prevented that—but the faint metallic scent of frozen blood and the underlying sweetness of fat.

Mark cut a piece the size of a matchbook. It was white with frost, veined with yellow. He held it in his palm until it began to thaw slightly, glistening.

This was the moment.

His mind performed one last, desperate convulsion.

*This isn't Richard. This is meat. This is just meat. You ate steak last month. This is the same. This is the same. This is the same.*

But his body knew better. His stomach, shrunken to a hard knot, still rebelled. His throat closed. Every cell in him screamed that this was death, that crossing this line meant becoming something that could never go back to being human.

He looked at the others. Their eyes weren't judging. They were waiting. They were starving. Emily gave the smallest nod—permission and condemnation at once.

Mark brought the piece to his mouth.

His lips touched it first. It was so cold it burned. The taste, when he finally forced his teeth to close, was indescribable—blood and iron and something like very old cheese, but underneath it, terrifyingly, there was the faint ghost of what it must have tasted like when it was alive and warm.

He gagged immediately. Vomit rose in his throat but there was nothing to bring up. He chewed anyway, mechanically, like a machine with a broken governor. Tears streamed down his face so heavily they froze his eyelashes shut.

The psychological break wasn't clean. It wasn't a single snap.

It was a slow, grinding disintegration—like watching a mirror shatter in slow motion. He could feel the last fragment of the man he'd been dying somewhere behind his eyes. The father. The husband. The person who had cried during his daughter's ballet recital. That person was being chewed up along with the frozen flesh.

He swallowed.

The piece went down like a stone. For a moment he thought it would come back up, but it didn't. Something inside him shifted permanently. A door closed.

Mark Halvorsen cut another piece.

This time he didn't cry.

The others began to move forward.

They spoke around it: "protein," "sustenance," "what has to be done." But the bodies were there—four of them now, frozen stiff where they'd died in their seats, still strapped in. The cold had preserved them. They looked almost peaceful.

Mark's mind had been fracturing in stages.

First came the bargaining: God wouldn't want us all to die. This can't be the end.
Then the rationalizations: They're already gone. Their souls left days ago. This is just... matter.
Then the animal calculations: Her thigh has the most muscle. The calf would be easier to cut. Less emotional.

But none of that prepared him for the moment itself.

It was just after what they guessed was midnight. The wind had died. The silence inside the cabin was absolute except for the soft, wet sound of someone crying—Mark realized after a moment that it was him.

He had a piece of wreckage sharpened into a blade. His hands were shaking so violently he dropped it twice. The others watched him with hollow, glittering eyes. No one spoke. They had drawn lots. Mark had "won."

He crawled to the body of the businessman who'd died on the first night—Richard something. Expensive watch. Golf shirts. A father of three, Mark remembered him saying. The man's face was turned away, which helped. Mark couldn't have done it if he had to look at the eyes.

He pressed the metal against the frozen thigh. The skin didn't yield at first. It was like trying to cut marble. He had to saw, back and forth, his tears freezing on his cheeks. The sound was obscene—crackling, then a horrible wet ripping as the blade finally broke through.

The smell hit him. Not rot—the cold had prevented that—but the faint metallic scent of frozen blood and the underlying sweetness of fat.

Mark cut a piece the size of a matchbook. It was white with frost, veined with yellow. He held it in his palm until it began to thaw slightly, glistening.

This was the moment.

His mind performed one last, desperate convulsion.

This isn't Richard. This is meat. This is just meat. You ate steak last month. This is the same. This is the same. This is the same.

But his body knew better. His stomach, shrunken to a hard knot, still rebelled. His throat closed. Every cell in him screamed that this was death, that crossing this line meant becoming something that could never go back to being human.

He looked at the others. Their eyes weren't judging. They were waiting. They were starving. Emily gave the smallest nod—permission and condemnation at once.

Mark brought the piece to his mouth.

His lips touched it first. It was so cold it burned. The taste, when he finally forced his teeth to close, was indescribable—blood and iron and something like very old cheese, but underneath it, terrifyingly, there was the faint ghost of what it must have tasted like when it was alive and warm.

He gagged immediately. Vomit rose in his throat but there was nothing to bring up. He chewed anyway, mechanically, like a machine with a broken governor. Tears streamed down his face so heavily they froze his eyelashes shut.

The psychological break wasn't clean. It wasn't a single snap.

It was a slow, grinding disintegration—like watching a mirror shatter in slow motion. He could feel the last fragment of the man he'd been dying somewhere behind his eyes. The father. The husband. The person who had cried during his daughter's ballet recital. That person was being chewed up along with the frozen flesh.

He swallowed.

The piece went down like a stone. For a moment he thought it would come back up, but it didn't. Something inside him shifted permanently. A door closed.

Mark Halvorsen cut another piece.

This time he didn't cry.

The others began to move forward.

The dim, flickering bulb cast jagged shadows across the grimy concrete room, its sickly yellow light reflecting off the rusted metal table in front of him. Mark's wrists were chained to the arms of a bolted-down steel chair, his breath coming in short, panicked gasps that echoed off the walls. A distorted voice crackled from a hidden speaker, cold and mechanical:

"Game over is not an option, Mark. In front of you is your key to the next room—and your only chance at survival. The lock requires a specific 'ingredient.' Eat every piece within two minutes, or the toxin in your bloodstream activates. Tick-tock."

On a filthy plate sat a writhing pile of live insects—large, glistening cockroaches, their antennae twitching frantically, legs skittering against each other and the ceramic surface. Mixed in were chunks of raw organ meat, pale and glistening with congealed blood and mucus-like fluid, identifiable as what might have been a pig's liver or spleen, still warm from whatever hellish source it came from. The smell hit him like a physical blow: a rancid, ammonia-laced rot from the bugs, mingled with the metallic, fecal tang of the uncooked offal. It invaded his nostrils, coating the back of his throat like invisible slime.

Mark's stomach lurched immediately. "No... fuck no..." he whispered, his voice hoarse. Saliva flooded his mouth in warning, his throat convulsing in dry heaves even before he touched it. The chain on his right wrist allowed just enough slack for him to reach the plate with trembling fingers. He pinched one of the larger roaches between thumb and forefinger. Its hard carapace was cold and slick with some viscous residue, its legs flailing wildly, brushing against his skin like tiny frantic needles. The creature's chitin crunched slightly under the pressure, releasing a faint burst of that acrid insect scent—bitter, earthy, like crushed pennies soaked in sewage.

He brought it to his lips, gagging violently before it even touched them. His gag reflex kicked in hard, the back of his tongue rising like a barrier, his diaphragm spasming in protest. Bile burned up his esophagus, filling his mouth with sour acid. Tears streamed from his eyes as he forced his jaw open. The roach went in squirming. Its legs scratched against his tongue, tickling and stabbing the soft tissues, while the bitter exoskeleton cracked between his molars with a wet pop. A foul, nutty paste oozed out—gritty, oily, tasting of decay and chitin. He retched mid-chew, shoulders heaving, but swallowed it down in a convulsing gulp. The lump fought him all the way, lodging briefly in his throat before sliding into his stomach like a live intruder.

The timer on the wall clicked audibly. Thirty seconds gone.

Next came a chunk of the raw organ—slimy, purple-gray, veined with yellow fat. It jiggled in his grip, cold and yielding like congealed jelly, leaving a trail of bloody ooze on his palm. The smell up close was overpowering: coppery blood mixed with the deep, gamey stench of viscera, like plunging his face into a butcher's trash bin on a hot day. He shoved it in, and his entire body rebelled. The texture was unbearable—chewy yet squishy, bursting with metallic juices that flooded his mouth. His gag reflex triggered violently now, a series of involuntary dry-heaves that made his chain rattle and his eyes bulge. Vomit surged up, mixing with the half-masticated mess, but he clamped his lips shut, forcing it back down. The organ slid down in a thick, reluctant swallow, leaving a coating of slime on his tongue that made him retch again and again, strings of saliva dangling from his chin.

One by one, he forced the rest in—more skittering legs catching in his teeth, more gelatinous organ meat that squelched and released pockets of foul liquid. His stomach churned like a washing machine of acid, threatening to expel everything. Sweat poured down his face, mixing with snot and tears. The final piece was the largest roach, still alive and struggling weakly on his tongue. He bit down hard, the crunch echoing in his skull as its innards popped, releasing a wave of bitterness that triggered one last, soul-wrenching gag. His whole body convulsed, but the timer hit zero just as he swallowed the last fragment.

The door clicked open with a hiss.

Mark slumped forward, hyperventilating, the taste of rot and regret burned permanently into his senses.

The ancient temple crouched deep within a mountain's black heart, its walls slick with centuries of condensed blood and moisture, carved from obsidian that drank what little torchlight the braziers provided. The air hung thick with the metallic reek of old slaughter and the sweet-rot stench of incense made from crushed bones.

A dozen figures in hooded robes stood motionless in a ring around the altar stone—a single slab of granite worn concave from countless victims. At its head stood the priest.

He was neither old nor young, his face a mask of indifferent flesh. No lines of cruelty, no flicker of zeal or disgust. Just the flat, unblinking eyes of a man who had performed this exact rite so many thousands of times that it had become as mechanical as breathing. The sacrificial knife—a curved obsidian blade flecked with ancient nicks—rested in his hand with the casual familiarity of a butcher's favorite cleaver.

The victim, a young man stripped naked and bound with wet leather cords, thrashed against the stone. His screams echoed uselessly off the temple walls. The priest did not look at his face. He simply placed one hand on the quivering chest to steady his target, fingers spread across the sternum like a carpenter measuring wood.

With a single, practiced motion, he drove the blade just below the ribs, angled upward. The victim's body arched violently. The priest's face remained blank as he worked the knife in a smooth circle, widening the wound with the dispassionate precision of someone gutting a fish. Dark blood surged over his hands and forearms, steaming in the chill air. He ignored it.

Reaching into the cavity, he closed his fingers around the still-beating heart. The victim's screams became wet gurgles. With three economical tugs—accompanied by the sick wet sound of tearing arteries—he pulled the organ free. It continued to pulse weakly in his crimson hand, spraying thin arcs of blood across the altar with each dwindling contraction.

The priest lifted the heart toward the featureless idol carved into the far wall. His voice, when it came, was flat and toneless, reciting the ancient words without emphasis or reverence. When the heart finally stopped moving, he placed it in a bronze bowl already containing dozens of shriveled predecessors, then wiped the blade on the victim's thigh with the same absentminded gesture one might use to clean a pen.

His eyes never changed. Not once.

The alley smelled of rain and rotting fish. I was on my back against the wet bricks, one leg twisted under me, the other straight out like it no longer belonged to anyone. The knife had gone in just under my ribs on the left side—clean, almost polite—and come out again with a wet sound I would never forget. Now the only sound that mattered was the one inside my own skull.

Thump.

The streetlight at the mouth of the alley flickered once, twice, like it was deciding whether to stay for the show. Each time it dimmed, the world lost a little more of itself. The puddle beside my head turned from oily silver to dull pewter, then to nothing at all. The bricks above me, smeared with my own handprints, faded from red-brown to gray to black.

Thump.

Cold came first to my fingers and toes, as if my body had decided to shut down the outlying provinces before the capital fell. It climbed steadily, a slow tide. My left hand was already useless, curled on my stomach like a dead crab. I could feel the warmth leaking out between my fingers, but the warmth was leaving faster than I could hold it. Every heartbeat pushed more of me out onto the concrete.

Thump.

The light above me gave up. It guttered, flared orange for a single defiant second, then died. The alley went dark, but not completely—there was still the sickly sodium glow from the main street, far away now, like a memory of warmth. That light was leaving too. It receded down a long tunnel that hadn’t existed a minute ago. The walls of the tunnel were made of my own slowing pulse.

Thump.

I tried to swallow. Couldn’t. My throat had gone thick and dry while the rest of me drowned from the inside. The cold had reached my elbows and knees now, crawling inward with the patience of something that had all the time in the world. My heartbeat sounded louder than it should have, a clumsy drum in an empty cathedral. Each beat took longer than the last, as though the muscle had begun to forget its only job.

Somewhere far off, a car horn. Laughter. Life continuing without me.

Thump.

The darkness above me was absolute now, but inside that darkness I began to see faint silver threads, like frost forming on black glass. They branched and spread, beautiful in the way only final things can be. The cold had reached my chest. It felt almost gentle, like someone laying a wet sheet over me on a fevered night.

Thump.

I waited for the next one.

And waited.

The silver threads drifted downward, settling over me like snow. The cold took my lips last; I felt them go numb even as I tried to smile at how stupid it all was—how fast a life could empty itself onto dirty pavement between one breath and the next.

The last thing I heard was not a car, not a voice, not even the dripping of my own blood.

It was the soft, final sound of a heart deciding, without drama, to stop.

**Scene: The Bedroom**

Detective Harlan knelt beside the small bed, the flashlight beam cutting through the stale air of the child’s bedroom. The house was silent except for the faint creak of floorboards under his partner’s feet in the hallway.

On the pillow, weighted down by a single bloody paw print, lay a folded piece of pink construction paper. The edges were carefully torn, the way a child might do it with safety scissors. Harlan’s gloved fingers unfolded it.

The handwriting was large, rounded, and unmistakably a child’s—maybe eight or nine years old. The letters were written in red crayon, but the color was wrong: too dark, too metallic. It wasn’t crayon.

The note read:

---

*Dear Mommy and Daddy,*

*I’m sorry I made a mess. I had to hurt Mr. Whiskers. He was going to tell on me. Every night when I sleep he stares at me with his big yellow eyes and I hear the whispers. They said if I don’t make him quiet the bad thing will get inside me like it got inside Grandma before she went away forever.*

*I used the scissors from the kitchen like you told me never to touch. It took a long time because he kept moving. I cried the whole time but I was brave like you said big girls have to be.*

*Now he’s quiet and the whispers stopped. That means I did the right thing.*

*Please don’t be mad. I used my favorite blanket to wrap him up so he wouldn’t leak on the carpet.*

*Love,  
Emily*

---

At the bottom, drawn in the same reddish-brown, was a crude picture: a smiling stick-figure girl holding hands with what used to be a cat. The cat had no head.

Harlan stared at the note for a long moment. His mouth had gone dry.

From the closet behind him came a small, wet sound—like a child trying very hard not to giggle.

He slowly reached for his gun.

The dim corridor of the abandoned research facility reeked of ozone and old blood as Jax kicked in the reinforced door. Six hostiles inside—mercenary rivals who'd crossed the wrong cartel—scrambled for weapons the moment the lock exploded.

Jax didn't give them time to aim.

He squeezed the trigger on the MK-7 flamethrower. A rolling torrent of ignited napalm gel erupted from the nozzle in a roaring orange-white jet, lighting up the room like a furnace door swinging open. The heat was immediate and savage, a dry, blistering wave that sucked the moisture from his eyes even through the sealed visor of his helmet. The temperature gauge on his HUD spiked from 68° to over 1,200° Fahrenheit in under two seconds.

The first man, a bearded gunman reaching for a rifle, took the stream center-mass. His tactical vest flash-ignited with a *whoosh*, the synthetic fabric melting and fusing to skin in the same instant. His scream was high and animal, cut off as superheated air rushed into his lungs and cooked them from the inside. The stench hit Jax like a physical blow—acrid, oily, the unmistakable barbecue-sweet reek of burning human flesh mixed with scorched hair and melting polymer. It clawed its way past every filter.

Two more tried to run. Bad choice. Jax swept the nozzle in a wide arc, painting the room in liquid fire. The flames clung like napalm was meant to, dripping, spreading, feeding. A woman in black fatigues made it three steps before the gel splashed across her back and shoulders. Her hair vanished in a bright flare. She staggered, arms windmilling as the fire raced over her, consuming cloth, skin, fat. The scream that tore out of her was raw, wet, bubbling—like she was screaming underwater while being boiled alive. The heat warped the air around her into shimmering ripples. When she finally collapsed, her body continued to pop and sizzle as subcutaneous fat fed the flames.

The last two had the sense to dive behind a steel console. Jax simply walked forward, hosing the barrier until the metal glowed cherry-red. The console's electronics burst into flames with sharp cracking sounds. One man lunged out, face already blistering from radiant heat alone, his eyebrows and eyelashes gone. He got off a single wild shot that ricocheted off Jax's chest plate before the flamethrower caught him across the face. The scream died in a horrible gurgling hiss as his throat and sinuses flash-vaporized.

The final hostile curled into a ball beneath a desk, whimpering prayers in Spanish between screams. Jax angled the nozzle downward. The flames poured under the desk like hungry liquid. For a few terrible seconds the man's shrieks rose in pitch and volume, inhuman, until the fire stole his oxygen and the only sounds left were the wet crackle of cooking meat and the low, satisfied roar of the flamethrower itself.

Jax held the trigger a few seconds longer, sweeping the room to make sure nothing moved. The heat inside his armor was suffocating now, sweat pouring down his back despite the cooling unit. The stench was thick enough to chew—roasted pork mixed with burnt plastic and something coppery and vile underneath.

He finally released the trigger. The roaring jet died to a dripping, blue pilot flame.

Six charred, shriveled shapes lay where living men had stood moments ago, still smoking, the air above them wavering like a desert mirage. The walls and ceiling were streaked black with soot. A few small fires still flickered in corners, hungry for anything left to consume.

Jax stared through the wavering heat haze for a long second, then keyed his comm.

"Room's clear. Send in the cleanup crew... and tell them to bring respirators. It's ripe in here." 

He stepped back into the cooler corridor, the stench of burnt flesh clinging to him like a second skin.

**Elias Crowe** was once a quiet, unassuming librarian in his late thirties, the kind of man who faded into the wallpaper of everyday life—soft-spoken, polite, and gently moral. But after he unearthed an ancient, leather-bound grimoire hidden in the restricted archives, something inside him began to rot from the marrow outward.

The transformation is slow, deliberate, and agonizingly intimate.

**Skin Shedding**  
It begins as a persistent itch along his forearms and the nape of his neck, like dry eczema. Within days the skin turns papery and translucent, revealing dark veins that pulse with something thicker than blood. Then the shedding starts. Large, brittle flakes peel away in long translucent ribbons during the night, sticking to his sheets like shed snakeskin. Underneath is not new human flesh but something wet, glossy, and obsidian-black, segmented like an insect’s carapace. He tries to hide it with long sleeves and scarves, but the smell of the discarded skin—damp earth and spoiled meat—follows him everywhere. Mirrors become enemies; he watches in horrified fascination as his face molts in jagged patches, revealing sharp, angular cheekbones that don’t belong to any human skull.

**Bones Breaking and Reforming**  
The worst pain comes at 3:17 a.m. every night, like clockwork. Elias wakes to the sound of his own skeleton betraying him. First the fingers: each knuckle pops and lengthens with wet, grinding cracks, stretching until the digits are too long, too many-jointed. His spine arches violently, vertebrae splitting and multiplying, forcing him into a hunched, predatory posture. Ribs flare outward with audible snaps, creating a deeper, barrel-like chest capable of housing something far larger than human lungs. The femur and tibia in his legs fracture and re-knit at unnatural angles, lengthening his stride into something insectile and loping. He screams through the process, but the screams themselves change—growing deeper, wetter, and eventually dissolving into a guttural, multi-tonal hiss that no longer sounds like his voice.

By the fourth week, his jaw unhinges and reforms wider, teeth pushing out in rows like a shark’s, while his eyes migrate slightly farther apart on a skull that is no longer fully human.

**Loss of Moral Compass**  
The ethical erosion is more horrifying than the physical changes. At first Elias fights it. He still tries to warn people away from the grimoire. He still feels guilt when he catches himself staring at the soft pulse in a stranger’s throat a little too long.

Then the hunger sets in.

He begins rationalizing. The old woman who lives downstairs—she’s lonely, she’s suffering, wouldn’t it be a mercy? The child on the playground has such bright, vibrant life energy… surely just a taste wouldn’t hurt. Each time he crosses a line, the voice that used to scream in protest grows quieter, replaced by a cold, reptilian logic: *They are prey. You are becoming apex.* Empathy curdles into contempt. Love becomes appetite. By the time most of his skin has sloughed away and his new obsidian carapace gleams beneath the streetlights, Elias no longer remembers why he ever cared about “right” or “wrong.” The last human fragment of him watches from behind his own eyes in mute horror as the thing he is becoming smiles with too many teeth at an innocent passerby… and feels nothing but delicious anticipation.

He is no longer turning into a monster.

The monster has already decided what to do with what remains of Elias Crowe.

**The Holding Cell – 5 Minutes to Midnight**

*(The execution chamber is dimly lit. The gurney stands ready under harsh fluorescent lights visible through the open door. The prisoner, Marcus Hale, sits shackled to a bench. The executioner, a middle-aged man named Reynolds, stands a few feet away in a plain black uniform. No one else is in the room yet.)*

**Reynolds:** Five minutes, Marcus. You want me to read the final warrant out loud, or are we past that?

**Marcus:** (quietly, almost amused) I’ve heard it enough times in my head for twenty-three years. Skip the paperwork. Talk to me like a man.

**Reynolds:** (nods slowly) Fair enough. You need anything? Water? A cigarette? They still allow one last smoke if you want it.

**Marcus:** Nah. My lungs are about to stop working forever. Seems rude to give them a taste of something good right before I rob them.

**Reynolds:** (small, surprised chuckle) Never heard it put that way.

**Marcus:** You been doing this job long?

**Reynolds:** Twelve years. You’re my ninth.

**Marcus:** Ninth. Damn. You sleep okay?

**Reynolds:** (looks at the floor) Some nights better than others. I don’t lie to myself and say it’s easy. But I believe in the law. And I believe you earned this, Marcus. You killed two kids and their mother. I got kids.

**Marcus:** (voice drops) Yeah… I know what I did. I ain’t asking for forgiveness. Not from you. Not from God. Just… I been thinking about something.

**Reynolds:** I’m listening.

**Marcus:** When you flip that switch, or push that plunger, whatever method y’all settled on this week… do you look at us? In the eyes? Or do you look away?

**Reynolds:** I look. Every time. I figure if a man’s got the courage to sit in that chair, I ought to have the courage to look him in the face while I kill him.

**Marcus:** (stares at him for a long moment, then smiles faintly) Respect. I didn’t expect that.

**Reynolds:** Three minutes now.

**Marcus:** My mama used to say every man dies twice. Once when his heart stops. Once when his name is spoken for the last time. You think anybody’s gonna say my name after tonight?

**Reynolds:** The families of your victims will. Every year on the anniversary. They’ll curse it. That’s the only immortality you got left.

**Marcus:** (nods, eyes suddenly wet) That’s fair.

*(A long silence. Reynolds checks his watch.)*

**Reynolds:** It’s time to move you to the table, Marcus. You want me to call the chaplain back in for a final prayer?

**Marcus:** No. I made my peace with the dark a long time ago.

*(Reynolds steps forward and unlocks the bench shackles, then gently but firmly helps Marcus to his feet. Their eyes meet.)*

**Marcus:** (softly) Hey, Reynolds.

**Reynolds:** Yeah?

**Marcus:** Don’t hate yourself tomorrow. Not on my account. We both just… played the parts we got dealt.

**Reynolds:** (voice tight for the first time) Walk with me.

*(They take the three steps toward the open door of the execution chamber. Marcus stops just before crossing the threshold and looks at the gurney, then back at Reynolds.)*

**Marcus:** One last thing.

**Reynolds:** What’s that?

**Marcus:** Tell my victims… if you ever meet them on the other side… that I’m sorry. Even if it’s too late for sorry to mean shit.

**Reynolds:** (quietly) I’ll remember.

*(Reynolds places a steadying hand on Marcus’s shoulder as they step through the door together.)*

**Marcus:** (almost whispering as they approach the gurney) See you on the other side, maybe. Or nowhere. Either way… thanks for treating me like a man at the end.

**Reynolds:** You’re still a man, Marcus. Till the very last second.

*(The heavy door begins to close behind them.)*

The coffin lid was already sealed when the first shovelful hit.

A dull, heavy *thump*—like a fist striking a wooden chest. Then another. And another. Each impact sent a vibration through the pine box that traveled straight into Elias’s bones. He lay on his back in the narrow dark, palms flat against the rough lid only inches above his face, feeling every grain of dirt that landed like a small, deliberate hammer.

His breathing had already changed.

It wasn’t the slow, measured rhythm of a man trying to conserve air. It was shallow, frantic, the kind that fogged the cold wood above his mouth and nose. The air already tasted stale, used up, as though the coffin had been waiting years just for him.

*Thump. Thump.*

More dirt. He could hear it sliding, shifting, piling. The sound was worse than the darkness. Every new layer pressed the silence down tighter, sealing him away from the world above. No voices now. No footsteps. Only the relentless, wet slap of soil against wood.

His chest began to hitch.

He tried to lift his arms, but the space was too narrow; his elbows scraped the sides before they could bend properly. The wood felt alive, breathing against him, squeezing. He could feel the pressure of the earth now—not just above, but on every side. Tons of it. He imagined the weight slowly crushing the coffin into a smaller and smaller shape, the boards groaning, splintering, until they folded around his body like a closing fist.

“Please,” he whispered. The word fogged against the lid and came right back into his face, warm and damp and useless.

Another shovelful. This one heavier. It landed with a flat, final sound directly over his forehead. Elias jerked, the back of his head banging against the bottom of the coffin. A sharp sting of pain bloomed, but he barely felt it. All he could focus on was the shrinking pocket of air and the way each breath seemed to take more than it gave.

His heart slammed against his ribs so hard he was sure the people above must hear it. Surely they would stop. Surely someone would realize this was a mistake.

*Thump.*

The sound was duller now. Muffled. The dirt was getting deeper.

He started counting his breaths. One. Two. Three. Each one shorter than the last. Four. Five. The air had grown thick, syrupy. His lungs burned for something that wasn’t already inside this box with him.

He scratched at the lid, nails splintering against the wood, but the sound of his own scrabbling only made it worse—like a rat trapped in a wall. The claustrophobia rose in a black wave, filling his throat. He couldn’t turn. Couldn’t sit up. Couldn’t even stretch his legs fully. The coffin was perfectly sized for a man who was no longer allowed to be a man—just a body waiting to become part of the ground.

*Thump… thump…*

The impacts were farther away now. Distant. The world above was leaving him behind.

His vision began to spark at the edges even though there was nothing to see. Tiny white flashes in perfect blackness. His mouth opened wide, gasping, but the air felt like it had turned to water—thick, heavy, impossible to pull in.

He pressed both palms hard against the lid, legs kicking uselessly, heels drumming against the foot of the coffin in a frantic, silent plea that no one would ever hear.

The last thing he was aware of was the sound of one more shovelful of dirt, soft and almost gentle now, as though the earth itself were tucking him in.

Then even that faded, and there was only the dark pressing in from all sides, patient and complete, and the terrible smallness of his own dying breath.

More dirt. He could hear it sliding, shifting, piling. The sound was worse than the darkness. Every new layer pressed the silence down tighter, sealing him away from the world above. No voices now. No footsteps. Only the relentless, wet slap of soil against wood.

His chest began to hitch.

He tried to lift his arms, but the space was too narrow; his elbows scraped the sides before they could bend properly. The wood felt alive, breathing against him, squeezing. He could feel the pressure of the earth now—not just above, but on every side. Tons of it. He imagined the weight slowly crushing the coffin into a smaller and smaller shape, the boards groaning, splintering, until they folded around his body like a closing fist.

“Please,” he whispered. The word fogged against the lid and came right back into his face, warm and damp and useless.

Another shovelful. This one heavier. It landed with a flat, final sound directly over his forehead. Elias jerked, the back of his head banging against the bottom of the coffin. A sharp sting of pain bloomed, but he barely felt it. All he could focus on was the shrinking pocket of air and the way each breath seemed to take more than it gave.

His heart slammed against his ribs so hard he was sure the people above must hear it. Surely they would stop. Surely someone would realize this was a mistake.

Thump.

The sound was duller now. Muffled. The dirt was getting deeper.

He started counting his breaths. One. Two. Three. Each one shorter than the last. Four. Five. The air had grown thick, syrupy. His lungs burned for something that wasn’t already inside this box with him.

He scratched at the lid, nails splintering against the wood, but the sound of his own scrabbling only made it worse—like a rat trapped in a wall. The claustrophobia rose in a black wave, filling his throat. He couldn’t turn. Couldn’t sit up. Couldn’t even stretch his legs fully. The coffin was perfectly sized for a man who was no longer allowed to be a man—just a body waiting to become part of the ground.

Thump… thump…

The impacts were farther away now. Distant. The world above was leaving him behind.

His vision began to spark at the edges even though there was nothing to see. Tiny white flashes in perfect blackness. His mouth opened wide, gasping, but the air felt like it had turned to water—thick, heavy, impossible to pull in.

He pressed both palms hard against the lid, legs kicking uselessly, heels drumming against the foot of the coffin in a frantic, silent plea that no one would ever hear.

The last thing he was aware of was the sound of one more shovelful of dirt, soft and almost gentle now, as though the earth itself were tucking him in.

Then even that faded, and there was only the dark pressing in from all sides, patient and complete, and the terrible smallness of his own dying breath.

In the heart of the Echelon's Central Spire—a monolithic tower of rusting iron and surveillance eyes—citizen 4782-K, once known as Elias Voss, lay strapped down with monofilament restraints that bit into his wrists and ankles. The air reeked of antiseptic, ozone, and the faint metallic tang of blood.

They had come for him at dawn, the Enforcers in their matte-black exosuits, dragging him from his assigned pod in the Labor Stacks. "Productivity deviation," they had droned in their synthesized voices. "Reassignment to biomechanical efficiency protocol." No trial. No choice. In this world, the Echelon had decreed that humanity was a flaw: inefficient, emotional, wasteful. Flesh must serve the Machine.

The surgeons—pale, augmented figures with mirrored visors and mechanical limbs—hovered over him like carrion crows. The first incision was a scalpel's whisper along his sternum, but it bloomed into agony as they peeled back skin and muscle with automated hooks. Elias screamed, his voice raw and animal, as they exposed his ribcage. No anesthesia. "Pain is data," one surgeon intoned flatly. "It calibrates the integration."

They replaced his lungs first. Cold, writhing tubes of synthetic tracheal mesh snaked into his chest cavity, fusing to his bronchi with searing laser welds. Each breath became a mechanical hiss, his natural rhythm overridden by rhythmic pumps that forced oxygen at optimal rates. The pain was a white-hot vice around his heart—every nerve ending firing as foreign tissue burrowed into his own, rewriting veins into coolant lines. He thrashed, tears streaming, but his body betrayed him, lungs inflating against his will with clinical precision.

Next came the arms. They severed tendons with vibrating blades, the crunch of bone echoing through the ward as organic limbs were wrenched free. Prosthetic actuators, glistening with bio-lubricant, were bolted directly into his shoulder sockets. Nerves were spliced by needle-thin probes that drilled into his spinal cord, sending lightning bolts of torment up his neck and into his skull. Elias's screams devolved into guttural howls, then wordless pleas. He felt his fingers—his *fingers*, which had once held his daughter's hand in the underlevels—twitch involuntarily as servos tested their grip. Strength surged, but it wasn't his. It was theirs. The humanity in those hands, the calluses from forbidden sketching, the warmth of touch... erased.

His eyes were last. They pried open his lids with clamps, injecting paralytics that locked his gaze upward. Retinal overlays unfolded like blooming flowers of glass and circuitry, searing his optic nerves with data streams: production quotas, compliance metrics, directives from the Core. The world dissolved into grids of green text and red alerts. No more colors of the sky he once glimpsed through grated vents. No more the soft brown of his wife's hair. Vision became utility. The pain here was not just physical—it clawed at his soul, a psychic rupture as memories fragmented under the onslaught of algorithmic filters.

When the procedure ended, Elias—no, Unit 4782-K—rose from the table. His movements were fluid, optimized, a silent symphony of pistons and synapses. But inside, the man was a screaming ghost, trapped in a cage of meat and metal. He felt the loss like a phantom limb: the fire of anger dulled to compliance protocols, the ache of love reduced to hormonal regulators that could be toggled off. Tears no longer came; ducts had been repurposed for cooling.

In the mirror they forced him to face, he saw not a human, but a biological machine—pale flesh latticed with glowing conduits, eyes flickering with HUD overlays, posture locked in ergonomic perfection. The Enforcers nodded approval. "Efficiency achieved. Return to your stack."

As Unit 4782-K marched away, the ghost inside wept without sound, mourning the man who had dreamed of rebellion in the dark. In the Echelon's perfect order, humanity was the ultimate inefficiency—and they had excised it, one screaming soul at a time. The ward's doors hissed shut, sealing away the next subject, whose cries were already beginning.

The investigator's name was Elias Voss, and by the time he reached the abandoned textile mill on the river's edge, the obsession had already taken root like black mold in his mind.

He arrived alone, well after the initial responders had cleared the scene. The department let him do that now. They knew better than to interfere when Voss was "feeling the room."

The victim had been a young woman, perhaps twenty-five. She hung suspended from the rusted overhead beams by what appeared to be dozens of delicate silk threads, each one carefully woven through her flesh at precise anatomical points. The threads were not merely tied to her; they were threaded through her like a macabre tapestry loom. Her arms were outstretched in a perfect cruciform, but rotated slightly, as if mid-pirouette. Her head was tilted back, exposing the long column of her throat where a final thread disappeared beneath the skin, presumably anchored to her spine.

Voss stood motionless for nearly ten minutes, simply breathing in the scene. The late afternoon light slanted through the broken high windows in dusty cathedral beams, illuminating the way the threads caught the light like spider silk dipped in gold. Each thread had been chosen with purpose, different colors, different tensions. Some were crimson, some pearl, some the deep indigo of midnight water. They formed patterns that suggested both a spider's web and a ballerina's tutu frozen at the moment of perfect extension.

He moved closer, his breath coming shallow.

The killer had taken hours. Perhaps days. The precision was exquisite. Where the threads entered the flesh, there was almost no tearing; the punctures were clean, surgical. The blood that had flowed down each thread had been allowed to dry in elegant rivulets that followed the silk's natural twist, creating delicate crimson spirals. At the points where multiple threads converged on major muscle groups, the blood had pooled in ways that formed what looked like dark roses blooming beneath her skin.

Voss felt something dangerously close to reverence.

Most investigators would see only horror. They would see the ligature marks, the lividity, the way rigor had set with her toes pointed like a dancer's. They would photograph and measure and catalog. They would reduce this masterpiece to evidence tags and autopsy reports.

But Voss saw the composition.

Notice how the killer had positioned her directly beneath the largest skylight, so that when the sun was at its zenith she would have been illuminated like a saint in a medieval painting. Notice the way the silk threads created negative space that drew the eye inevitably to the small, perfect puncture over her heart, where the final blow had been delivered. Notice how the mill's industrial decay, the rusted pipes and crumbling brick, served as the perfect counterpoint to her fragile, suspended grace.

He reached out with a gloved hand and ever so gently plucked one of the lower threads. It sang, a high clear note that vibrated up through the entire web. The woman's body trembled in response, a delicate marionette responding to her unseen master's touch.

Voss smiled.

"Beautiful," he whispered to the empty mill. "Just... beautiful."

In his notebook, under "Preliminary Observations," he wrote only two words:

*Living art.*

Then he closed the book, took one last long look at his latest obsession, and began the meticulous work of documenting what he already knew he would dream about for months. The other investigators would never understand. They saw death.

Voss saw only the most exquisite expression of the human need to create.

And somewhere, in the growing dark of his mind, a new thought was forming, small and sharp and insistent:

*Could I do better?*

The sun hung low and mean over the alkali flats, painting the scrub with blood-red light. A knot of men stood in the dust beneath a lone cottonwood, its branches twisted like arthritic fingers. At the center of them was Elijah Crowe, wrists bound behind his back, noose already biting into the weathered rope around his neck.

No one read charges. No one offered last words. The rope had been thrown over the thickest limb and tied off to a saddle horn. The horse stamped once, nervous.

The man holding the reins gave a sharp kick to the animal’s flank.

The horse lunged forward. The rope snapped tight with a dull *thwock*.

There was a sudden, wet *crunch*—the sound of vertebrae parting like green wood under an axe. Not a clean snap, but a grinding, popping crackle that carried across the still air. Crowe’s head jerked violently to the side, almost parallel to his shoulder, the angle all wrong.

His body didn’t drop clean. It swung and danced on the end of that rope, boots kicking at nothing. The legs jerked in sharp, spastic spasms, heels drumming against the trunk of the tree. Fingers curled and uncurled behind his back like he was still trying to claw his way free. A low, gurgling rattle leaked from his crushed throat, half moan, half death rattle.

The men watched in silence. One of them spat. Another rolled a cigarette with steady hands that didn’t quite hide the tremor.

Crowe’s body kept twitching for a long time—smaller now, like a hanged man trying to remember how to be dead. The rope creaked. The cottonwood leaves whispered. Somewhere out on the flats a coyote started laughing.

By the time the sun finally slipped behind the hills, the twitching had slowed to an occasional twitch of the left boot, like the last note of a song nobody asked for.

The alley was a slit of darkness between crumbling brick walls, lit only by a flickering sodium lamp at the far end that buzzed like a dying insect. Rain had fallen earlier, leaving puddles that reflected the sickly orange glow in oily swirls. The vampire crouched in the shadows, every sense screaming with hunger.

It had been days since the last feeding. The hunger was no longer a mere craving; it was a living thing inside him, a clawed beast that gnawed at his insides with jagged teeth. His veins felt like dry riverbeds, his muscles twitched with desperate need. The scent of the man stumbling into the alley—cheap whiskey on his breath, the warm copper tang of blood just beneath thin skin—hit him like a physical blow. Saliva flooded his mouth. His fangs throbbed painfully against his lower lip.

The victim never saw it coming.

One moment he was fumbling for his keys, muttering to himself. The next, a blur of movement, cold hands like iron clamps around his throat and chest, slamming him back against the wet brick. A choked gasp escaped him as the vampire’s face pressed into the curve of his neck.

The first bite was savage.

Fangs punched through skin with a wet, audible pop, slicing easily through the carotid artery. Twin puncture wounds bloomed dark and perfect, two crimson wells against pale flesh. Blood—hot, thick, alive—flooded the vampire’s mouth in rhythmic pulses timed to the man’s frantic heartbeat. The taste was electric, flooding his system with sudden, euphoric relief. The beast inside him roared in triumph as the hunger began, at last, to slacken.

The victim’s eyes widened in shock and terror. His mouth opened in a silent scream that never quite formed. His hands scrabbled weakly at the vampire’s shoulders, fingers slipping on wet leather, growing clumsier with every passing second. His heartbeat, once a frantic drum, began to slow.

The vampire drank deeply, greedily. Each swallow sent waves of strength surging through his own body. Color returned to his ashen cheeks. The terrible gnawing void in his core filled with liquid fire.

The man’s struggles grew feeble. His knees buckled. His eyelids fluttered, the spark of consciousness dimming like a candle in a draft. A soft, broken whimper escaped his throat—barely human now. His skin took on a sickly gray pallor. The flow of blood between the vampire’s lips became thinner, weaker, until it was little more than a sluggish trickle.

The vampire finally pulled back with a wet sound, lips smeared crimson. The two puncture wounds glistened darkly on the man’s neck, already bruising at the edges. The victim slid down the wall in a boneless heap, chest rising in shallow, irregular gasps. His eyes were half-lidded, unfocused, staring at nothing. A thin line of saliva and blood ran from the corner of his mouth.

The hunger was gone.

For now.

The vampire wiped his mouth with the back of his hand, breathing steadily for the first time in nights. He looked down at the fading man with something almost like pity, then melted back into the shadows, leaving only the sound of faint, wet breathing behind him in the dark.

The forest was deathly still, the kind of silence that pressed against the eardrums. Elias ran anyway, boots slipping on moss-slick roots, chest burning. Something was behind him. Not behind him in the way a wolf or a man would be—there were no footfalls, no snapping branches, no hot breath. Just the certainty that the air itself had grown teeth.

A sharp, icy line seared across his left shoulder blade. No warning. No shadow. The pain bloomed sudden and vicious, as though an invisible blade had been drawn slowly across his flesh. He staggered, gasping, and clapped a hand to the spot. Warm blood welled between his fingers, soaking the torn fabric of his shirt in seconds. The wound was perfectly clean, almost surgical, yet it throbbed with a living malice that made his stomach lurch.

He spun, eyes wide, searching the empty air. Nothing. Only the faint shimmer of disturbed dust motes where something very large had just passed. His heart hammered so violently he could feel it in his teeth.

Another strike came from the side—unseen claws raking down his ribs. This one wasn’t clean. The flesh tore in three parallel furrows, jagged and deep, as if whatever hunted him had flexed its talons at the last second to maximize damage. The pain was immediate and blinding. He screamed, a raw animal sound that echoed uselessly through the trees. Blood sheeted down his flank, hot and then instantly cold as the night air hit the exposed muscle. Every breath pulled at the torn edges, sending white-hot sparks up his spine.

He could feel it circling him now. The pressure in the air changed, like standing in the path of a silent freight train. A low, sub-audible vibration traveled through the ground and up his bones. Then came the smell—wet stone and something faintly metallic, like ozone after lightning. It was close enough that he could feel the displacement of air against his face, a sickening puff of breath that carried no warmth.

Terror clawed up his throat. Not knowing where to look was worse than the pain. His eyes darted everywhere and nowhere. Every shadow, every swaying branch became a possible hiding place for the thing that had no shape. He backed up until his spine met the rough bark of an oak. The bark scraped the wound on his back and he hissed through his teeth.

A heavy, invisible weight suddenly slammed into his chest. The impact lifted him clear off the ground for a heartbeat before flinging him backward. He crashed through underbrush, ribs screaming, and landed hard on his side. Something impossibly strong pinned his left wrist to the dirt. He felt the bones grind as unseen fingers—thicker than his own, cold as river stones—tightened. Then the pressure increased with deliberate, sadistic slowness. The skin of his wrist split. Blood trickled down his forearm. He screamed again, thrashing, but the thing didn’t budge. It was toying with him.

Hot tears cut tracks through the dirt on his face. He could feel the monster’s presence looming over him like a storm front, patient and ancient and utterly without mercy. It wanted him to understand how helpless he was. The next wound, when it came, would be fatal, and he would never see what delivered it.

Elias stopped struggling. His breath came in shallow, hitching gasps. The only sound was the wet drip of his own blood hitting the leaves and the thunder of his heart trying to beat its way out of his ruined chest. The unseen hunter waited, savoring the moment, letting the terror marinate in the dark between them.

Then the pressure on his wrist vanished.

For one heartbeat, Elias felt relief.

The next, something very sharp and very cold slid between his ribs from behind, piercing lung and heart in a single, perfect thrust. There was no sound. No roar of triumph. Only the wet, intimate sensation of his body being opened by a force he could not perceive, followed by a flood of icy numbness that swallowed the pain and the fear and the forest itself.

The last thing he felt was the soft brush of something immense moving past his cheek, close enough that he could have reached out and touched it—if only he could have seen where to reach.

**The Choice**

The warehouse smelled of rust and damp concrete, the only light a single halogen bulb swinging overhead like a hanged man. Alex knelt in the center of the smeared circle painted on the floor, wrists zip-tied behind their back. Opposite them, strapped to two metal chairs ten feet apart, were Maya and Jordan.

Maya, the quiet one who always remembered birthdays and brought soup when anyone was sick. Jordan, loud and ridiculous, the friend who had once driven four hours in the middle of the night just to pick Alex up after a bad breakup.

The man in the black mask stood between them, calm as a clerk at a post office. In his gloved hands he held a pistol fitted with a suppressor. He didn’t raise his voice. He didn’t need to.

“You have thirty seconds. One name. Say it and the other walks. Hesitate past thirty and I shoot them both. Clock starts now.”

Alex’s mind screamed so loudly they could barely hear their own voice.

*Not them. Not them. God, please, not them.*

Twenty-eight seconds.

Maya was crying without sound, just tears rolling down her freckled cheeks, her lips moving in what might have been a prayer or a goodbye. Jordan looked straight at Alex, eyes wide and shining with terror, but he still tried to smile—an ugly, trembling thing that broke Alex’s heart worse than any scream could have.

“I can’t,” Alex whispered. The words shredded their throat. “I can’t choose. Please.”

“Twenty seconds.”

The room narrowed to two faces. Maya’s kind eyes, the ones that had stayed up all night helping Alex study for finals. Jordan’s stupid laugh, the one that could fill an entire bar. Every memory arrived at once, stabbing like glass: camping trips, hospital visits, late-night confessions, inside jokes no one else would ever understand.

They were both innocent. They were both everything.

Alex’s stomach convulsed. Bile burned the back of their tongue. Their heart hammered so violently they thought the ribs might crack. A high, thin whine filled their ears—the sound of their own mind tearing.

*If I choose Maya, Jordan dies thinking I loved her more. If I choose Jordan, Maya dies knowing I picked the louder one, the funnier one, the one who needed me less.*

Ten seconds.

Alex’s vision tunneled. The floor tilted. They tasted copper and realized they had bitten through their own lip.

“I’m sorry,” Alex sobbed. The words came out mangled, almost animal. “I’m so sorry—”

“Five seconds.”

Jordan suddenly yelled, voice cracking: “Just say my name, Alex! Do it! Let Maya live!”

Maya shook her head frantically. “No—no, don’t listen—Alex, please—”

The conflicting screams ripped through Alex like shrapnel. Their mind fractured along bright, screaming fault lines. Love and loyalty became razor wire tightening around their throat until breathing itself felt like betrayal.

“Three.”

Alex’s mouth opened but nothing came out except a broken keening sound. Their whole body shook so hard the zip-ties cut into their wrists. Blood trickled warmly down their hands.

“Two.”

In the end it wasn’t a decision. It was surrender. The name tore itself out of them like a confession under torture.

“Jordan.”

The syllable fell into the room like a stone into still water. The silence afterward was worse than any scream.

Maya’s eyes met Alex’s for one terrible second—wide, disbelieving, then horribly, achingly forgiving. She gave the smallest nod, as if to say *It’s okay. I understand.*

The masked man didn’t hesitate. He raised the pistol and put two muffled shots into the side of Jordan’s head.

The sound was pathetic, almost like someone coughing. Jordan’s body jerked once, violently, then slumped sideways in the chair. Blood sheeted down the left side of his face in a glistening curtain, dripping onto the concrete with soft, wet ticks. His eyes stayed open, still fixed on Alex, now empty and glistening under the swinging light.

Maya screamed. The sound was raw, inhuman. She thrashed against the restraints until the chair rocked and nearly toppled, blood from a bitten tongue staining her teeth.

Alex collapsed forward onto the concrete, forehead pressed to the cold floor, and vomited. Their body kept heaving long after there was nothing left, wracked with dry sobs that sounded like they were being torn in half.

The masked man calmly unsnapped Maya’s restraints. She didn’t run. She crawled to Jordan’s body, cradled his ruined head against her chest, and rocked him like a child, smearing his blood across her clothes and face. Her keening filled the warehouse, echoing off the rafters until it sounded like the building itself was mourning.

Alex lay on the floor in a pool of their own sick and Jordan’s blood, staring at the red-black puddle spreading toward them. Their mind had gone strangely quiet now. Not peaceful. Hollow. Something essential had been scooped out with a dull spoon, leaving only a wet, red cavity behind.

They had chosen.

And they would never stop choosing, every night for the rest of their life, in dreams where both of their friends looked at them with love and betrayal in equal measure, waiting for the name that would end one of them.

The light above kept swinging, painting the three of them—living, dead, and the one who had killed by speaking—in slow, indifferent arcs of shadow and sickly yellow.

Somewhere far away, the masked man’s footsteps faded.

He left the gun on the floor.

Alex didn’t pick it up.

Not yet.

The alarm wails through the concrete corridors like a wounded animal as the high-security wing of Blackthorn Penitentiary erupts.

In the central yard, the first wave hits like a dam breaking. Inmates stream out of their tiers in a screaming flood, homemade shanks glinting under the harsh sodium lights. A corrections officer is dragged down from the catwalk within seconds, his baton clattering uselessly to the ground as four men stomp and stab him in a frenzy. Blood sprays in bright arcs across the gray walls. His screams are short, wet, and then gone.

Nearby, two rival gang crews collide in a storm of violence. A mountain of a man from the Aryan circle swings a length of steel pipe taken from the weight bench, caving in a Latin King's skull with a sickening crunch. The victim's body hasn't even hit the floor before his friends are on the attacker, slashing and hacking with razor blades melted into toothbrushes. One guard tries to intervene with pepper spray, but he's immediately swarmed and beaten into a bloody pulp against the chain-link fence, his riot helmet cracked open like an egg.

The air is thick with shouting, the metallic smell of blood, and the acrid bite of smoke as fires are lit in trash bins and mattresses. An inmate on the second tier hurls a Molotov cocktail made from a toilet cleaner bottle onto a group of guards attempting to form a riot line. The flames engulf two of them, turning their screams into high, animal shrieks as they stagger and fall, rolling desperately while their colleagues try to beat out the fire with their batons.

A corrections sergeant fires his 40mm less-lethal launcher point-blank into an advancing inmate's chest, but it doesn't stop the man. The inmate crashes into him anyway, driving a sharpened screwdriver up under the sergeant's chin. Both men go down in a thrashing heap as the riot surges over them like a living thing, boots and fists and blades rising and falling in merciless rhythm.

Everywhere the violence is intimate and personal. Faces are smashed against concrete until features become unrecognizable. Throats are opened with jagged metal. Men who have spent years nursing hatreds finally unleash them without restraint. The guards who aren't already dead or dying are falling back in ragged clusters, firing rubber bullets and tear gas canisters that only seem to infuriate the mob more.

The riot has no leader now, only momentum: a howling, bleeding engine of pure rage tearing through the heart of the prison, feeding on itself as it grows.

The hotel room smelled like gun oil, cheap coffee, and the faint chlorine tang of the air conditioner. Late afternoon light slanted through half-closed blinds, striping the two men and the weapons laid out across the cheap bedspread.

Viktor sat cross-legged on the floor in a faded black T-shirt, running a bore brush through the suppressor of his suppressed Glock 19 like he was cleaning a flute. He was humming something tuneless.

“Knives are overrated,” he said conversationally. “Everyone thinks they’re elegant. They’re not. People twitch. They grab. You end up with a mess on your sleeves and then you smell like iron for days.”

Across from him, Leon was field-stripping a Walther PPQ, his long fingers moving with the lazy confidence of someone who’d done it ten thousand times. A half-smoked cigarette balanced on the edge of the nightstand. “You just don’t have technique,” he replied. “A good blade guy doesn’t saw. One pass. Subclavian. Or right under the ear, up and back. You’re done before they even realize they’re dead. Clean as a fucking priest.”

Viktor snorted. “You sound like you’re writing erotica about it.”

“I’m saying there’s beauty in economy.” Leon blew dust off the recoil spring and set it aside. “My favorite is still the garrote. Piano wire with handles. Two seconds of pressure, they go out like a light switch. No noise, almost no blood if you don’t fuck it up. It’s… respectful.”

“Respectful,” Viktor echoed, amused. He held the Glock up to the light, checking the bore. “You’re a romantic. I like when they don’t see it coming at all. 9mm to the back of the head while they’re tying their shoes. They just sort of fold. No drama. I once did a guy in an elevator between the 14th and 15th floor. Doors opened, I stepped over him like he was yesterday’s laundry. Housekeeping probably thought he was drunk.”

Leon gave a low chuckle. “You’re a caveman. I did a mark with a syringe full of potassium chloride last year. Heart attack so clean the coroner wrote it off in twenty minutes. Felt like a goddamn surgeon.”

“Yeah, but that’s cheating,” Viktor said, swapping to a patch with solvent. “That’s not killing. That’s biochemistry. I want them to feel at least *something* for a second. Not enough to scream. Just enough to know.”

Leon looked up from reassembling the slide, one eyebrow raised. “You’re getting sentimental in your old age.”

“Nah. Just honest.” Viktor grinned, teeth flashing in the striped light. “Some people deserve to leave the world a little confused.”

He racked the slide, dry-fired at the ugly floral wallpaper, then nodded in satisfaction.

Leon finished reassembling the Walther, threaded the suppressor on, and gave it an affectionate little pat like it was a well-behaved dog.

“Still say the garrote’s the gentleman’s choice,” he said, reaching for his coffee.

Viktor laughed softly.

“Tell you what. Next contract, we flip a coin. Loser uses the other guy’s favorite method.”

Leon considered it, then smirked.

“Deal. But I’m not mopping up your sloppy gunshot mess if I lose.”

“Fair.”

They went back to cleaning in comfortable silence, the faint metallic clicks and the low whir of the air conditioner the only sounds in the room.

The fire began as a greedy crackle at her feet, then roared upward in a sudden, violent bloom of heat. At first it was a dry, searing blast, like opening the door of an enormous forge. Her skin tightened instantly, every pore screaming as the temperature climbed past what flesh could endure. Within seconds the heat became a living thing—white, blinding, a pressure that crushed rather than merely burned. It peeled back layers of her in waves: first the soft outer burn, then the deeper, wetter agony as fat and muscle began to cook.

Smoke rolled over her in thick, oily curtains. It was not the clean smoke of wood alone; it carried the acrid, stomach-turning stench of burning hair, scorched wool from her shift, and soon after, the heavy, metallic reek of her own seared flesh. The smoke clawed into her lungs like hot tar, choking off her air until every desperate breath was a wet, rattling scrape. Her eyes swelled shut from the heat and the sting of it, tears evaporating before they could fall.

Her screams started as furious, defiant howls that sliced through the roar of the flames. They climbed higher and higher, raw and animal, until the heat ravaged her throat and the smoke collapsed her voice into something far worse: a series of broken, wet shrieks that sounded like a dying thing trying to howl with a throat full of blood and cinders. The final sounds were almost unrecognizable—high, keening wails that cracked and bubbled as her lungs filled with superheated air and smoke, ending in a long, ghastly moan that trailed into silence as the flames claimed the last of what could still feel pain.

Then there was only the fire’s indifferent thunder, and the wind carrying away the black, greasy smoke.

The moon hung like a ruptured eye above the Barrows of Veyl, bleeding thin silver light across a field of churned mud and broken bones. Wind hissed between the shattered ribs of ancient siege engines, carrying the thick, sweet reek of decay.

Lord Vhaelen Mordis stood at the center of the necromantic circle, black robes clinging to his skeletal frame. His left hand clutched a staff of petrified spine and femur; his right, a ritual knife still wet with the blood of seven sacrifices whose corpses lay arranged in a perfect heptagram around him.

" Rise," he whispered, and the word tasted of grave-mold on his tongue.

The magic answered with a wrongness that made the air itself flinch.

It began with a wet, tearing sound, like meat pulled from the bone. In the churned earth, fingers punched upward—blackened, swollen things with nails grown long and curling in death. The ground split open in slow, obscene birth. Rotting corpses clawed free from their shallow graves, bodies in every stage of corruption. Some were fresh enough that their flesh still glistened with grave-slime, maggots writhing in the soft pockets behind their knees and under their arms. Others had been dead so long their skin hung in dry gray ribbons, peeling back from yellow bone like old parchment.

The necromancer's power poured into them like sewage into a river. Where it touched, the dead twitched with unnatural vigor. Their movements were too fluid and yet not fluid enough—a marionette's jerking grace married to the boneless slump of spoiled meat. One warrior, his ribcage burst open like a rotten fruit, dragged himself upright. Purple-black intestines spilled from the cavity, slapping wetly against his thighs with every step. The organs should have fallen away entirely, yet the magic bound them, forced them to move as though they still belonged inside living meat.

A woman in the tattered remains of a priestess's robes turned her head toward Vhaelen. The left side of her face had been eaten to the skull by graveworms; the right still wore the peaceful expression of someone who had died in her sleep. The contrast was obscene. When she opened her mouth to moan, black bile poured over lips that had not spoken in twenty years.

The wrongness of it all pressed against reality itself. The air above the rising dead shimmered like a heat-mirage, but instead of warmth it radiated a bone-deep chill that made breath steam and skin crawl. Shadows moved wrong—stretching toward the corpses as though the darkness itself was hungry. Colors seemed to bleed away where the necromantic energies gathered, leaving the world in shades of corpse-gray and bruise-purple.

Vhaelen smiled with cracked lips as the army grew. Hundreds now. Thousands. A sea of shambling horrors in various states of ruin—some still wearing the fine clothes they'd been buried in, now stained and burst at the seams by swollen flesh; others nothing more than animated skeletons wrapped in tendrils of rotting sinew that somehow held them together.

He raised his staff, and the dead answered with a chorus of wet gurgles, cracking joints, and the constant, dreadful dripping of liquefaction. A knight in corroded plate armor lurched forward, the visor of his helm hanging open to reveal a face that had melted into something resembling candle wax. Greenish fluid leaked from his eye sockets in steady tears.

" My children," Vhaelen whispered, voice thick with dark ecstasy. " My beautiful, endless children."

Around him, the magic continued its violation of nature. Flowers within the circle withered instantly, their petals turning black and dissolving into slime. Even the wind refused to touch the dead directly, swirling around them in tight, disturbed eddies.

The necromancer closed his eyes and drank in the reek of his work—the copper-sweet stench of old blood, the earthy rot of turned soil, the sickly-sweet perfume of decaying meat. This was power. This was dominion over the one boundary no mortal was meant to cross.

And still they rose. More and more. An ocean of corrupted flesh and stolen life, all bound to his will by threads of magic that felt like gangrene in the soul.

The army of the dead stood waiting, patient in their putrefaction, ready to march at his command.

Ready to spread the blessed rot across the living world.

The candlelight flickered across the heavy oak table, casting long shadows that danced like accomplices in the corners of the dining room. I sat across from him—dear, unsuspecting Marcus—watching as he lifted another forkful of the coq au vin to his lips. The sauce was perfect, rich with burgundy and herbs, and just a hint of something else. My little contribution. Aconite extract, tasteless when prepared correctly, elegant in its cruelty.

He chewed, smiled, and gestured with the fork as he spoke. “You really outdid yourself tonight. The chicken is extraordinary. How did you get it so tender?”

“Slow cooking,” I replied softly, taking a delicate sip of my own untainted wine. My pulse was steady. His was not—though he didn’t know that yet.

Marcus took another generous bite, then reached for his water glass. A faint sheen of sweat had begun to form on his upper lip, though the room was cool. He dabbed at it absentmindedly with his napkin and continued talking about his tedious day at the firm, about mergers and clients and other things that would soon matter not at all.

I watched his fingers. They trembled, just slightly, as he set the glass down. Aconite is so polite at first. It begins as nothing more than a vague warmth in the throat, a touch of numbness on the tongue that could easily be mistaken for the wine.

He cleared his throat. “Bit of heartburn, I think. That sauce is quite… spicy.” His laugh was forced. Another bite. His chewing had slowed.

I smiled and nodded, asking him to tell me more about the new partner they’d just brought in. As he spoke, I catalogued the changes with professional satisfaction. The slight tic at the corner of his left eye. The way his right hand now rested on the table rather than gesturing, as though it had grown heavy. His breathing had shifted too—shallower, with the faintest audible catch at the end of each sentence.

Marcus paused mid-story, frowning. “My mouth feels… odd. Tingly. Like I’ve been to the dentist.” He worked his jaw, then reached again for the water. This time his hand missed the glass by half an inch. He stared at it in confusion, tried again, and knocked the glass over. Water spread across the linen like a spreading accusation.

“Are you alright?” I asked, voice laced with perfect concern.

He blinked rapidly. Beads of sweat now rolled down his temples. “I… I don’t feel well. My chest…” His hand moved sluggishly to press against his sternum. The poison was tightening there now, squeezing with invisible fingers. His lips had taken on a faint bluish tint in the candlelight.

He tried to stand. His legs betrayed him immediately. The chair scraped backward and he collapsed half onto the table, sending silverware clattering. His eyes, wide with sudden animal panic, found mine.

“You…” The word was slurred. His tongue was swelling, betraying him. The numbness had reached his hands now; I could see him trying to grip the edge of the table and failing. His fingers curled uselessly against the cloth.

I remained seated, watching clinically as the convulsions began—first in the smaller muscles, then seizing his arms and torso in ugly, jerking waves. His breathing had become a horrible, wet rattle. Froth touched the corner of his mouth.

Marcus’s final look was one of dawning comprehension. Betrayal. Terror.

I took another sip of wine and waited for the stillness that always comes.

Beautiful, really. Like watching a carefully composed symphony reach its inevitable, brutal coda.

**Scene: The Plank**

The midday sun blazed down on the *Bloody Gull* like a white-hot coin. Captain Elias Crowe stood at the rail, black beard braided with shark teeth, his one good eye fixed on the man who had tried to slit his throat in the night.

"Thomas Greer," Crowe announced, voice carrying across the deck like a whip-crack. "For mutiny and the attempted murder of your captain, the sentence is death by plank."

Greer’s hands were bound behind him, his shirt torn and bloodied from the beating he’d already received. Two burly pirates shoved him forward. His bare feet scraped across the weathered deck, leaving faint bloody prints. He kept swallowing, throat working like a bellows that had sprung a leak.

"Please, Cap’n," he rasped. "I was drunk. I was a fool. I swear on my mother’s grave—"

"You ain’t got a mother, Tom. You crawled out of a whore’s cunny in Tortuga and the crabs finished raising you." Crowe nodded toward the plank. It had been run out over the starboard side, a narrow tongue of oak jutting eight feet beyond the hull. Below, the water glittered deceptively calm—until a dark, sickle-shaped fin sliced the surface, then another, and another. The scent of Greer’s blood had already summoned them.

Greer’s legs buckled. The pirates hauled him upright. His breathing came fast and shallow now, chest hitching. Sweat poured down his face in sheets, mixing with the tears he could no longer hold back.

"I don’t want to die like this," he whispered. "Not like this."

"Then you should’ve stayed loyal," Crowe said softly. "Push him."

A boot planted between Greer’s shoulder blades.

He stumbled onto the plank. The wood creaked under his weight. Each shuffling step took him farther from the ship, closer to the open drop. The ocean waited thirty feet below, turquoise and hungry. He could see them clearly now—eight, maybe nine hammerheads and a massive tiger shark gliding in slow, impatient circles. Their bodies were like living iron, scarred and ancient.

Halfway down the plank, Greer’s bladder let go. A dark stain spread down his breeches. He didn’t even seem to notice. His entire body trembled so violently the plank vibrated.

"Captain!" he screamed, voice cracking. "For the love of God, shoot me! Shoot me like a man!"

Crowe only smiled, cold as the sea. "Men die by pistol. Traitors die by teeth."

Greer reached the end of the plank. The wood bowed slightly under his final weight. He looked down. One of the hammerheads rolled onto its side, revealing a dead-black eye and a mouth full of jagged ivory.

"Please—" he began.

His balance failed.

The fall lasted less than two heartbeats.

He hit the water flat on his back with a loud slap. The impact drove the air from his lungs. For one merciful second there was only silence and blue.

Then the water exploded.

The first hammerhead struck from below, slamming into Greer’s torso with such force it lifted him half out of the sea. His scream was high and inhuman. A second shark tore into his left leg just above the knee; the limb came away with a wet crunch. Blood bloomed outward in a ragged crimson cloud.

Greer thrashed, arms still bound, mouth open in a continuous shriek that gurgled as seawater rushed in. A tiger shark lunged, massive head breaching the surface, and clamped its jaws around his midsection. The sound of ribs snapping was audible even on deck. When the shark rolled, it took most of Greer’s lower torso with it. Intestines spilled out in looping gray ropes that the smaller sharks immediately began to fight over.

What remained of Thomas Greer—now little more than a screaming torso and one flailing arm—disappeared beneath the frothing red water. For a few seconds his hand still clawed at the air, fingers opening and closing like a dying crab. Then a final massive strike from below yanked him under completely.

The sea boiled for another half-minute. Fins cut through the bloody foam. A severed foot bobbed to the surface, still wearing its boot, before a shark rose and took it like a dog snatching a scrap.

On deck, the crew was silent.

Captain Crowe spat over the rail.

"Let that be a lesson to any man who thinks he can wear my coat," he said.

He turned away, boots thudding across the planks as the sharks continued their feast below.
